scenario: Price has tested the same resistance level twice in the last two hours. Volatility (ATR) is rising and the 20 EMA is above the 50 EMA.
note: Repeated tests of a level with rising volatility and an aligned trend have historically favored continuation more often than reversal in this synthetic sample — but the edge is modest, which is why WAIT still beats SELL comfortably.

scenario: Price just spiked through the prior day's high on a news release, then immediately gave back two-thirds of the move within 15 minutes.
note: Fast post-news spikes that reverse sharply are a classic "fakeout" pattern. Chasing the initial breakout (BUY) scores worst here — the highest-EV choice is often simply not participating.

scenario: Price has been ranging sideways for six sessions between two well-respected levels, with no clear trend and below-average volatility.
note: Low-volatility, no-trend conditions rarely offer a clean directional edge. WAIT scores highest because there's no statistical reason to prefer a direction — this is a "no trade" setup by design.

scenario: Price has broken below a well-tested support level with expanding volume and is now retesting that same level from below.
note: A "break and retest" of support from below, on expanding volume, is one of the more consistent continuation setups in this puzzle set — SELL has the clearest edge of any option here.

scenario: Price is chopping in a tight 15-pip range for the last 90 minutes right before a major central bank rate decision is due.
note: Pre-announcement chop ahead of a major rate decision is close to pure noise, and the coming volatility spike is unpredictable in direction. WAIT is the clear best decision.
